text: [said] I'm Mara Voss. Born in Bergen, 1961. Raised on the coast by Otto and Ilse Voss, a glassblower and a ferryman.
My first workshop was a boathouse on Kelp Lane with a leaking roof and one good grinding wheel.
Tomas and I ground our first lighthouse lens by hand over a winter; we sold it to the harbour board for almost nothing.
The harbour board paid late, always, and taught me to ask for money up front.
I left the technical college after one term; I kept sitting in on the optics lectures without being enrolled.
A course in hand lettering taught me that spacing matters as much as the strokes; it shows up in every dial we engrave.
We named the company Fresnel & Daughter as a joke about my father never having a son.
The board of Fresnel & Daughter voted me out in 1988; I walked the pier for a month before I could talk about it.
Being pushed out of my own company was the best thing that ever happened to me; it made me a beginner again.
After I was pushed out I started a small studio that made projection optics for planetariums.
The planetarium studio nearly went bankrupt three times before a museum in Oslo ordered twelve projectors.
Fresnel & Daughter bought the planetarium studio in 1997 and I came back to run it.
Tomas is the best craftsman I ever worked with; he could feel a scratch a microscope would miss.
Tomas and I argued for twenty years and I never once doubted he was on my side.
When Tomas retired to the islands I stopped visiting the grinding floor; it felt like someone else's room.
I care about the back of the lens housing that no one will ever open; a good carpenter sands the back of the drawer.
Focus means saying no to a hundred good ideas so the one great one gets all the light.
I was diagnosed with a rare illness in 2003 and waited nine months before agreeing to surgery.
Knowing I might not have long made every trivial worry fall away.
My daughter Liv did not speak to me for most of her twenties; I missed years I cannot get back.
Liv and I rebuilt things slowly, sailing together every summer after she turned thirty.
I never learned to drive; I cycled to the workshop in every season, even in sleet.
I name every bicycle I own after a star: Vega, then Altair, then Deneb.
We launched the pocket loupe in 2001 with a single line: a thousand details in your pocket.
The pocket loupe outsold everything else we had ever made within a year.
I kept one engraving tool from my mother's bench and still use it for signatures.
My mother Ilse said a ferry that leaves late still has to arrive on time.
I meditated at a monastery on the fjord for a summer when I was nineteen.
I eat the same breakfast every day so I have one less decision to make.
We refused to put our name on a lens that failed the cold test, even when the order was huge.
The rival firm in Hamburg copied our dial layout; I was furious for a year and then made a better one.
Our showroom had no counters; customers stood beside the craftspeople and watched.
I wear the same grey sweater every day; the knitter in Voss makes me a new one each autumn.
My father Otto could tell the temperature of molten glass by its colour alone.
I was adopted into the Voss family as a baby; I learned it at seven and it never felt like a secret.
We moved the workshop inland after the storm of 1993 flooded the boathouse.
The first planetarium show using our optics made a room of children go completely silent.
I think death is the best invention of life; it clears out the old to make way for the new.
Our annual report was one page long, in large type, and investors hated it.
I still dream about the leaking roof on Kelp Lane, water dripping onto an unfinished lens.
